title: Big hits and the race-record market
summary: 'Tippin' In' and 'After Hours' sold well, and he explains how race records differed from white bands' pop releases.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: Yeah. Well, you mentioned again the "Tuxedo Junction" thing. And well, that was your biggest hit, right?

Right. But you know, that "Tippin' In" and "After Hours" was very big, big sellers. They, they both were on the gold standard of Victor. Now, they put a certain amount of records out on that every year.
So, that was actually around 1939 that you became known as the Tuxedo Junction Orchestra with the theme song and all of that?
Now, back then, especially in the earlier times when you started recording, they were geared more or less to the race market. Is that correct?
Oh yeah. I see what you mean. Right. At that time, they were.
Yeah. Can you tell us a little bit about that?
Well, the only thing I could see at that time was like they used to distribute mostly the same tunes the black bands would make what they would call a race record.
And, the white bands had most of the top, top tunes, new tunes that they'd broadcast a lot. First of all, it was played straight. You know?

Then, they finally started giving, well, I got one of the first top tunes while I was with Victor - "I Don't Want To Walk Without You Baby", you know. Cause if I didn't use it, maybe Tommy Dorsey would have had it first.
But, they used to have the tunes
on a race record where the black bands would just make it practically anyway they wanted and have it jazzed up style like.
When they gave it to the other part, to the white bands, then they played it mostly straight where people could actually sing it, hum it, while we go for ourselves. You know?

What finally just broke right down during the time, I think I made "I Don't Want To Walk Without You Baby". It was in the 40's. And from then on, whatever tunes that, they used to send me tunes over to the theaters to comes down to record. And the other bands, I noticed there was a lot of other bands doing the same thing.
